title: Lumbini Monastic Zone, Monastery by Monastery
meta_description: A monastery-by-monastery guide to Lumbini's East and West monastic zones: who built each temple, which tradition, what to look for and how to plan the day.
summary: Lumbini's monastic zone is a planned avenue of temples built by Buddhist communities from around the world. Theravada monasteries stand in the East zone, Mahayana and Vajrayana ones in the West. Cycle it in a morning, starting early, and use the table below to choose six or seven to visit properly.

sections.heading: How the zone came to be
paras: In 1967 U Thant, the Burmese Buddhist diplomat who was then Secretary-General of the United Nations, visited Lumbini and found a neglected site in farmland. He pushed for an international effort to develop it, and the Japanese architect Kenzo Tange was commissioned to draw up a master plan, completed in the 1970s. Tange laid out a rectangle of about 4.8 by 1.6 km, aligned north to south, with the Sacred Garden at the southern end and a long central canal leading north.

The middle part of the plan is the monastic zone. Plots were offered to Buddhist countries and organisations to build monasteries in their own national styles. The canal divides it into two halves: the West Monastic Zone for the Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions, the forms of Buddhism followed in China, Korea, Vietnam, Japan, Tibet and the Himalaya, and the East Monastic Zone for the Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos. Building has gone on for decades and some plots are still under construction.

The result is unusual anywhere in the world: within a few kilometres you can walk from a Thai ordination hall to a Chinese palace-style monastery to a Tibetan stupa, and see how one teaching took the shape of many cultures.

sections.heading: The East Monastic Zone: Theravada
paras: Enter the East zone from the path along the canal, east of the Eternal Peace Flame. The Theravada tradition keeps the oldest surviving collection of the Buddha's teachings in the Pali language, and its monasteries tend to be simpler in decoration, with a single large Buddha image and wide, quiet halls.

The Royal Thai Monastery is the one most visitors remember: a gleaming building of white marble with stacked, swept-up Thai roofs, set in a formal garden. Inside, the shrine hall is bright and calm. Myanmar is represented by the Myanmar Golden Temple and by the Lokamani Cula Pagoda, a tall golden stupa modelled on the Shwedagon in Yangon. The Sri Lanka monastery is busiest in the winter season, when Sri Lankan pilgrim groups dressed in white arrive by the busload.

Many Theravada monasteries have resident monks who keep a strict schedule, with alms and meals before noon. Visit in the morning, keep your voice low and do not offer to shake hands with monks. Women should not touch a Theravada monk or hand objects directly to him; place them on a cloth or table instead.

sections.heading: The West Monastic Zone: Mahayana and Vajrayana
paras: Cross the canal by one of the bridges to the West zone. The buildings here are larger and more colourful. The Zhong Hua Chinese Buddhist Monastery is laid out like a Chinese imperial palace, with gates, courtyards, red columns and curving tiled roofs; it is one of the most photographed buildings in Lumbini. The Korean monastery, Dae Sung Shakya Sa, is a very large multi-storey hall that has taken many years to complete. Vietnam's Phat Quoc Tu has a tall pagoda and a gentle garden.

For Vajrayana, the Buddhism of Tibet and the Himalaya, visit the Great Drigung Kagyud Lotus Stupa, built with support from a German foundation, whose domed interior is covered in detailed murals. Nepal's own Himalayan Buddhists are represented by the Manang Samaj Stupa, built by the community from Manang district north of the Annapurnas. In these temples you will see prayer wheels, butter lamps, thangka paintings and images of Padmasambhava and Tara.
Some Vajrayana shrine rooms are closed outside prayer times. If a door is shut, ask a monk or caretaker politely; they often open it for a quiet visitor.

sections.heading: Reading the buildings as you go
paras: The zone is easiest to enjoy if you know a few things to look for. Start with the robes. Theravada monks from Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar wear saffron, ochre or deep orange. Tibetan and Himalayan monks wear maroon with yellow. Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monks and nuns usually wear grey or brown, often with shaved heads for both men and women.

Then the stupas. The Theravada stupa is a smooth bell rising to a tall spire, as in the golden Burmese pagodas. The Tibetan stupa, or chorten, sits on a stepped square base with a dome, a spire of rings and often painted eyes or symbols. The Chinese and Vietnamese pagoda turns the stupa into a tower of stacked roofs.

Inside, look at the hands of the main Buddha image. Fingers touching the earth recall the moment of awakening at Bodh Gaya; a raised open palm means protection and reassurance; hands resting in the lap mean meditation. In Vajrayana shrine rooms you will also see wrathful protector figures, which guard the teaching rather than threaten visitors, and many images of Tara, the female bodhisattva of compassion, in green and white forms.

sections.heading: The north end: museum, cranes and the Peace Pagoda
paras: Past the monasteries, the canal ends near the Lumbini Museum, which holds finds from Lumbini and the surrounding Kapilavastu area: coins, terracotta figures, pottery and stone sculpture, together with manuscripts and photographs. Nearby is the Lumbini International Research Institute, a library for scholars of Buddhism.

Just outside the northern boundary stands the World Peace Pagoda, a white dome with golden images of the Buddha set into its sides, built by the Japanese order Nipponzan Myohoji, which has built peace pagodas in many countries, including one above Phewa Lake in Pokhara. The wetlands around it form the Lumbini Crane Sanctuary, a protected habitat for the sarus crane, the tallest flying bird in the world, which nests in the farmland of Rupandehi and Kapilvastu. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times to see pairs feeding in the fields.

sections.heading: How to plan your day in the zone
paras: Distances are longer than they look on a map, and from March to October the heat is serious. Start by 7 am, visit the East zone first while monks are active, cross to the West zone before 10:30, and stop for lunch and rest during the hottest hours. Return in the late afternoon for the north end and the Peace Pagoda at sunset.

Most monasteries are free to enter, with donation boxes. A small offering is welcome but never required. Some monasteries offer simple guest rooms to pilgrims, and a few run meditation sessions; ask at the office.
list: Hire a bicycle near the main gate or through your hotel; e-rickshaws are the alternative
Carry water, a hat and slip-on shoes; you will remove them at almost every shrine
Expect monasteries to close for an hour or more around midday
Visit fewer temples slowly rather than all of them quickly
Keep to paths in the crane sanctuary and do not approach nesting birds

faqs.q: How many monasteries are in Lumbini?
faqs.a: Dozens of plots in the monastic zone have been allocated to Buddhist countries and organisations, and the number of finished monasteries grows every few years as new ones open. In a single day most visitors see six to ten properly. Rather than counting, we suggest choosing a few from each zone so you see Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana side by side.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the East and West monastic zones?
faqs.a: The central canal divides them. The East Monastic Zone holds Theravada monasteries, the tradition of Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand and neighbouring countries. The West Monastic Zone holds Mahayana and Vajrayana monasteries, the traditions of China, Korea, Vietnam, Japan, Tibet and the Himalaya. The arrangement was part of Kenzo Tange's master plan.

faqs.q: Which monasteries in Lumbini should I not miss?
faqs.a: For a first visit: the Royal Thai Monastery and the Lokamani Cula Pagoda in the East zone, the Zhong Hua Chinese monastery, the Korean temple and the Great Drigung Kagyud Lotus Stupa in the West zone, and the World Peace Pagoda at the north end. Together they show the range of Buddhist architecture well.

faqs.q: Do monasteries charge an entry fee?
faqs.a: Most monasteries in the zone do not charge an entry fee and have donation boxes instead. A small offering is welcome. The Sacred Garden and the museum have their own tickets. Rules can change, especially for newer buildings, so check current status before you travel or ask your guide on the day.

faqs.q: How do I get around the monastic zone?
faqs.a: Cycling is easiest: the zone is flat, paths are wide and you can stop wherever you like. Bicycles can be hired near the main gate and through hotels. E-rickshaws are the alternative and are good in the heat or for older travellers. Walking the whole zone is possible but long, especially from March onwards.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in a Lumbini monastery?
faqs.a: Some monasteries offer simple guest rooms to pilgrims, usually for a donation and with house rules on silence, meal times and dress. Availability changes and many prefer to host groups from their own country. Ask directly at the monastery office or through your guide, and have a hotel booked as a backup.

faqs.q: Can I join prayers or chanting at the monasteries?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, as a quiet observer. Many monasteries hold morning and evening chanting, and visitors may sit at the back. Remove shoes, sit with your feet tucked away from the shrine and monks, and keep phones silent. Ask before taking photos. Times vary by monastery, so your guide checks on the day.

faqs.q: What is the World Peace Pagoda in Lumbini?
faqs.a: It is a white, domed stupa just north of the monastic zone, built by the Japanese Buddhist order Nipponzan Myohoji as one of the peace pagodas it has raised in many countries. Golden Buddha figures are set in its sides. It is a popular place for sunset, and the Lumbini Crane Sanctuary lies around it.

Most open in the early morning and close at dusk, and many close for an hour or more at midday for meals and rest. Hours vary by monastery and on festival days. Visit the East zone first in the morning, when Theravada monks are active, and save the north end for late afternoon. Your guide will check current hours.
